title: Slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction
note: In the 1850s, every attempt to settle whether slavery could spread into the West made the conflict worse. Lincoln's election in 1860 led seven Southern states to secede, and four more followed once war began. The Union's victory in 1865 preserved the nation and ended slavery, and Reconstruction amendments promised citizenship and equal rights.

read.title: A house divided
text: By 1850 the North and South had grown apart. The North's economy rested on free labor and growing industry; the South's rested on cotton grown by enslaved people, who numbered nearly four million by 1860. The key political question was whether slavery could spread into western territories. The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state but included a harsh Fugitive Slave Act that angered many Northerners. In 1854 the Kansas-Nebraska Act let settlers vote on slavery, and Kansas erupted in violence. The new Republican Party formed to stop slavery's expansion, and in 1857 the Dred Scott decision declared that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

When Republican Abraham Lincoln won the presidency in 1860, South Carolina seceded, followed by ten more states. War began at Fort Sumter in April 1861. The Union had more people, factories and railroads, but the Confederacy fought on its own ground. In 1863 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and nearly 200,000 Black men served in the Union army and navy. After Gettysburg the South never regained the initiative, and Lee surrendered in April 1865.

During Reconstruction, three amendments ended slavery, made freed people citizens and protected Black men's voting rights. But when federal troops left the South in 1877, white-controlled governments steadily took many of those rights away.
